chunks: 1767 - Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Mūsā al-Riḍā عليه السلام wrote to Muḥammad ibn Sinān, in what he wrote as a response to his questions:

“The reason for sawm (fasting) is to know the touch of hunger and thirst, so that one may become humble, meek, rewarded, seeking reward, and patient. That also serves as a proof for him regarding the hardships of the Hereafter, along with what it contains of breaking him away from desires, acting as an admonisher for him in the immediate world and as a guide to the final abode, so that he may know the severity of the condition of the people of poverty and destitution in this world and the Hereafter.”

key_terms.الشَّهَوَاتِ: base desires and appetites restrained through fasting
key_terms.الصَّوْمِ: sawm; fasting as an act of worship
key_terms.الْآخِرَةِ: the Hereafter, whose hardships fasting helps one remember
key_terms.الْجُوعِ: hunger, physically experienced to cultivate awareness
key_terms.الْعَطَشِ: thirst, endured as part of spiritual discipline
key_terms.الْفَقْرِ: poverty, the condition fasting teaches one to understand

ai.seo_question: Why was fasting made obligatory in Islam according to Imam al-Riḍā عليه السلام?
ai.summary: This hadith explains that sawm (fasting) was prescribed so a person directly experiences hunger and thirst, cultivating humility, patience, and conscious seeking of divine reward. It also trains the soul against desires, reminds one of the hardships of the Hereafter, and deepens awareness of the suffering of the poor and destitute.
